Lorsqu’on évoque l’histoire du Canada, o: When Canadian history comes up, the history of Chinese immigrants tends to be forgotten. July 1 is Canada Day, but for members of the Chinese Canadian community, the date recalls decades of humiliation that left an indelible mark on their collective memory: on July 1, 1923, new Chinese arrivals were barred from entering Canada. For Asian Heritage Month, La Converse spoke with members of the community about the legacy of oppression Canada left the Chinese community.
« Bon premier mois de mai ! » s’exclame: “Happy first of May!” exclaims Timothy Chan, an 87-year-old Chinese Canadian, as he lifts his cup of tea to his lips, in the midst of the lively conversations and laughter of the elders around him. A longtime regular at the restaurant Ruby Rouge, he speaks in English with a Cantonese accent, in the warm setting of this establishment in Montréal’s Chinatown. For him, eating the Hong Kong cuisine of his childhood in this neighbourhood, where he has invested so much, has a special flavour this May. As he celebrates Asian Heritage Month, 2023 marks a turning point in his fight to shed light on the history of those he calls the “lo wah kiu” (the “old overseas Chinese”), because it is the centennial of the law that excluded them.
L’aîné de 87 ans plonge dans ses souveni: The 87-year-old dives into his memories. After a long pause, he pulls a sheet of paper covered in Chinese characters from his pocket, recording information he refuses to let sink into oblivion. After a moment of reflection, he lifts his cup with difficulty, spilling a little tea on the red tablecloth. “My uncle, my mother’s brother, suggested I leave for Canada. I accepted. He paid $1,700 to get the necessary documents,” Timothy recalls. In the early 1950s, $1,700 was the equivalent of about $20,000 today, a colossal sum for the son of a Chinese peasant from the city of Taishan.
À l’âge de 16 ans seulement, Timothy déb: At just 16 years old, Timothy landed alone on Canadian soil. The memories rush back as he recalls it. In a voice worn smooth by time, he tells the story. “At the time, there was no direct flight between Hong Kong and Canada. You went from Hong Kong to Japan by ship, then from Hawaii to San Francisco. After that I arrived in Canada by train, passing through Vancouver and Montréal.” His burning desire to be reunited with his grandfather, who had immigrated to the United States in search of financial stability, led him to undertake a journey of several months.
Chan est considéré comme l’un des dernie: Chan is considered one of the last living historical witnesses of the period of systematic oppression of Chinese people. From 1885 to 1947, the Chinese population was subjected to immigration legislation based solely on racial criteria. The period began with the imposition of a head tax, and from 1923 to 1947 it became one of outright prohibition of Chinese entry into Canadian territory. The policy persisted for years after its repeal, limiting Chinese immigration to the spouses and children of Chinese people who had obtained Canadian citizenship. It was not until 1967 that the restrictions linked to this legislation were officially lifted.

Le certificat d’immigration de la taxe d: The head tax certificate of William’s father, Hing Dere, showing he paid the $500 in 1921 to enter Canada.
Comme dans le cas de Timothy, la traject: As in Timothy’s case, the migration path of Chinese people during those terrible years often began with a heavy debt. From 1885 to 1923, a head tax was imposed to discourage Chinese people from settling in the white colony. “1885 is an important date, because that’s when construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway was completed,” says William Ging Wee Dere, a writer and historian and the author of the book Being Chinese in Canada. A hint of bitterness can be heard in the words of the third-generation Chinese Canadian: “There were a lot of Chinese workers looking for work. The European settlers thought there were too many Chinese workers. They couldn’t tolerate that.” The tax rose gradually, from $50 to $500 in 1903. Chinese people were forced to borrow money for a chance to protect their identity and ensure their survival within the nation.
« 500 $ représentaient une somme considé: “$500 was a considerable sum… At the time, it could have bought two houses. Many people, including my grandfather, were forced to borrow money.” William explains that families resigned themselves to paying such a sum because it was seen as an investment in the family’s future. In an era marked by the Second World War and the civil war in China, investing in the immigration of a healthy young Chinese man offered a glimmer of hope of escaping poverty.
<strong>L’isolement aux deux bouts de l’: Isolation on both sides of the ocean
En plus du fardeau financier, la séparat: On top of the financial burden, the family separation imposed by these immigration laws left a painful memory within the community. In a voice filled with sadness, William shares the following: “It was a very difficult situation, a very bad situation for my mother, who stayed in the village. Even though she wanted to come to Canada with my father, she couldn’t, because Canada didn’t allow immigration, even for family members.”
Pour sa mère, restée en Chine, la respon: For his mother, who stayed in China, the responsibility of providing for the family was heavy. She farmed land bought with money sent by her husband and her father-in-law, who had emigrated.
De l’autre côté du Pacifique, le sentime: On the other side of the Pacific, his father and grandfather shared the feeling of isolation. “My father went back to the village every 5 to 10 years. Every time he came home, my mother gave birth to children some time later. That’s how my brothers and sisters and I were born,” says William. It is estimated that in 1941, more than 29,000 Chinese men were living in Canada, 80% of whom had wives and children who remained in China. The white majority saw the Chinese community as a community of “married bachelors,” a reference to the situation of most Chinese men isolated in Canada.
Les seuls liens qui unissaient la famill: The only ties that held the family together were formed through exchanges of letters. “During that period, he wrote a lot, a lot of letters to my mother, along with the money he had to send to support the family,” William says. As with many immigrants, William’s story begins with a family separation. The family was only able to reunite in 1956, after the repeal of the Chinese Exclusion Act and the coming into force of the Canadian Citizenship Act, which allowed his father to acquire citizenship in 1950.
La famille de William devant la buanderi: William’s family in front of the Wing On laundry in 1957, in Montréal. William Ging Wee Dere is in the middle, in his cowboy outfit.
De la même manière, Timothy échappa à la: In the same way, Timothy escaped loneliness when he arrived in Montréal by finding refuge among other members of the Chinese community. He worked as a waiter at the restaurant Jardin du Cerf, and on his days off he spent his time reaching out to the owners of the city’s Chinese laundries. “I worked a whole week to get one day off. On that day, I didn’t go to the casino or to a nightclub. I went to the laundries to talk with the owners. I visited 400 laundries and talked with 400 people,” he says with a touch of pride.
Le récit de Timothy met en lumière la ré: Timothy’s story highlights the complex reality of immigration to Canada and is a reminder that arriving on foreign soil is only the starting point of a path toward integration. Among these immigrants, people like William’s grandfather and father chose to open laundries. These modest businesses turned into genuine cultural and social centres, playing an essential role in the flourishing of the Chinese community. As social and racial segregation grew in Canadian society, the nighttime gatherings of shopkeepers around a feast were, for these immigrants, a vital way to preserve their existence and to restore severed ties with their families in China.
Pour ces Sino-Canadiens, la commémoratio: For these Chinese Canadians, commemorating their past of exclusion carries a profound meaning for preserving their existence within Canadian society. William stresses the importance of remembering how long the community has been in Canada: “It is crucial for us to remind people that our community has been here for more than 150 years.” For Timothy Chan, commemorating these immigration laws is a reminder that must be made to the current Canadian government. In a booming voice that rises above the conversations filling the restaurant, he exclaims: “It’s an injustice. Today, they talk about human rights… But look, 100 years ago, did Canada care about human rights?” In 2006, the federal government officially apologized for the Chinese Immigration Act and granted $20,000 in compensation to surviving head tax payers and to their widows living in Canada.
Aujourd’hui, autant William que Timothy: Today, both William and Timothy define their sense of belonging to Canada through their experience of immigration. William identifies as Chinese Canadian, stating: “It is crucial to emphasize that I am Chinese Canadian, because I am not Euro-Canadian, or Franco-Canadian, or Anglo-Canadian. Even if people try to assimilate me into one of those societies, I refuse to be assimilated. My life is an act of resistance.” Similarly, Timothy fights to preserve his identity by valuing Chinese history. The octogenarian laments: “You never find these Chinese people of world history in books and newspapers, and that saddens me. I’d like to keep making them known, but I’m getting old.”
Faire connaître l’histoire des<em> lo wa: Making the history of the lo wah kiu known is also a way of informing newly arrived Chinese immigrants in Canada about their community’s historical struggles. William states the following: “I think it’s essential that recently arrived immigrants, whether they come from mainland China, Southeast Asia, Europe or elsewhere, understand the foundations of the struggle the Chinese community has waged throughout Canadian history for equal rights and historical recognition.”
Depuis des décennies, Timothy Chan s’app: For decades, Timothy Chan has worked to preserve the history of the loh wa kiu. As the founder of the discussion forum “The East Wind Society,” opened in 1959, his goal has always been to inform members of the Chinese community about current events so that they become aware of what he calls “world Chinese history.” Timothy declares solemnly: “The history of China is an essential part of world history. It is of great importance to the Chinese community, to Chinese people themselves, and it is also important to me.”
Puis il conclut, sur un ton résolu : « C: Then he concludes, in a resolute tone: “It’s not only for the Chinese community to know, but for all communities.” Timothy hopes that future generations, as well as other communities, will carry on the legacy of the Chinese Canadian community in Canada.
